label: Virology
blurb: Genome, envelope, and capsid — plus the syndromes and antivirals

organisms.name: Herpes Simplex Virus 1
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped double-stranded linear DNA, icosahedral capsid, replicates in the nucleus; Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells with Cowdry A intranuclear inclusions; PCR of CSF for encephalitis
organisms.manifestations: Gingivostomatitis, herpes labialis (cold sores), keratoconjunctivitis with dendritic corneal ulcers, temporal lobe encephalitis, herpetic whitlow, erythema multiforme
organisms.treatment: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir; foscarnet for thymidine kinase-mutant resistant strains
organisms.transmission: Respiratory secretions and saliva; direct contact with active lesions or asymptomatic shedding
organisms.virulenceFactor: Latency in the trigeminal ganglion with reactivation under stress, fever, or UV light; viral thymidine kinase is the target that makes acyclovir selective
organisms.tooltip: The most common cause of sporadic viral encephalitis, with a temporal lobe predilection and hemorrhagic necrosis on MRI. Latency sits in the trigeminal ganglion.

organisms.name: Herpes Simplex Virus 2
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped dsDNA virus; Tzanck smear with multinucleated giant cells; PCR of lesion swab or CSF; type-specific serology
organisms.manifestations: Painful genital vesicles and ulcers, aseptic meningitis (Mollaret), neonatal herpes with skin, eye, and mouth disease or disseminated infection
organisms.treatment: Acyclovir or valacyclovir for episodes and suppression; intravenous acyclovir for neonatal disease; cesarean delivery if active lesions at labor
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact including during asymptomatic shedding; perinatal transmission through an infected birth canal
organisms.virulenceFactor: Latency in the sacral ganglia with periodic reactivation and asymptomatic viral shedding that sustains transmission
organisms.tooltip: Latency in the sacral ganglia, versus trigeminal for HSV-1. Most transmission occurs during asymptomatic shedding, which is why partner history is often negative.

organisms.name: Varicella Zoster Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped dsDNA herpesvirus; multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck; PCR of vesicle fluid; lesions in different stages simultaneously in varicella
organisms.manifestations: Chickenpox with a centrifugal rash in crops at different stages; shingles in a single dermatome with postherpetic neuralgia; Ramsay Hunt syndrome; disseminated zoster in the immunocompromised
organisms.treatment: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset; live varicella vaccine and recombinant zoster vaccine for prevention
organisms.transmission: Respiratory aerosols and direct vesicle contact; airborne precautions are needed for varicella and disseminated zoster
organisms.virulenceFactor: Latency in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia; reactivation with waning cell-mediated immunity in age or immunosuppression
organisms.tooltip: Dermatomal distribution reflects reactivation in a single dorsal root ganglion. Lesions at different stages at once distinguishes varicella from smallpox, where all lesions are synchronous.

organisms.name: Epstein-Barr Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped dsDNA herpesvirus; positive heterophile (Monospot) antibody test; atypical lymphocytes (reactive CD8 T cells) on smear; infects B cells via CD21
organisms.manifestations: Infectious mononucleosis with fever, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, exudative pharyngitis, splenomegaly, and fatigue; associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and oral hairy leukoplakia
organisms.treatment: Supportive care and avoidance of contact sports for 3 to 4 weeks given splenic rupture risk; no antiviral indicated
organisms.transmission: Saliva — the kissing disease — with prolonged shedding after illness
organisms.virulenceFactor: Binds CD21 on B cells and immortalizes them via LMP-1 and EBNA; drives c-myc translocation in Burkitt lymphoma
organisms.tooltip: Giving amoxicillin produces a diffuse maculopapular rash — a classic exam clue, and not a true penicillin allergy. The atypical lymphocytes are reactive T cells, not infected B cells.

organisms.name: Cytomegalovirus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped dsDNA herpesvirus; owl's eye intranuclear inclusions on histology; negative heterophile test; PCR viral load for monitoring
organisms.manifestations: Heterophile-negative mononucleosis; retinitis, colitis, and esophagitis in AIDS with CD4 below 50; pneumonitis in transplant; congenital infection with periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, and jaundice
organisms.treatment: Ganciclovir or valganciclovir; foscarnet or cidofovir for UL97-mutant resistance; letermovir for transplant prophylaxis
organisms.transmission: Saliva, urine, sexual contact, breast milk, blood transfusion, and transplanted organs; transplacental for congenital disease
organisms.virulenceFactor: Latency in mononuclear cells; downregulation of MHC class I to evade cytotoxic T cells
organisms.tooltip: The most common congenital infection worldwide. Periventricular calcifications point to CMV; diffuse intracranial calcifications point to toxoplasmosis. Owl's eye inclusions are the histologic signature.

organisms.name: Human Herpesvirus 8
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped dsDNA herpesvirus; spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces on biopsy; immunostaining for LANA
organisms.manifestations: Kaposi sarcoma with violaceous plaques and nodules on skin, palate, or viscera; primary effusion lymphoma; multicentric Castleman disease
organisms.treatment: Antiretroviral therapy to restore immunity is the mainstay; chemotherapy such as liposomal doxorubicin for extensive disease
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact, particularly among men who have sex with men; saliva in endemic regions
organisms.virulenceFactor: Viral homologs of cyclin D and IL-6, plus a G-protein coupled receptor that drives VEGF-mediated angiogenesis and endothelial proliferation
organisms.tooltip: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor of endothelial origin, which is why lesions are violaceous. It can be confused with bacillary angiomatosis from Bartonella — biopsy distinguishes them.

organisms.name: Hepatitis B Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped partially double-stranded circular DNA, the only DNA virus using reverse transcriptase; serology of HBsAg, anti-HBs, HBeAg, and anti-HBc defines stage; ground-glass hepatocytes
organisms.manifestations: Acute hepatitis with jaundice, chronic hepatitis leading to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, polyarteritis nodosa, membranous nephropathy, serum-sickness-like syndrome
organisms.treatment: Tenofovir or entecavir for chronic infection; hepatitis B immune globulin plus vaccine for postexposure and neonatal prophylaxis
organisms.transmission: Parenteral, sexual, and perinatal; perinatal transmission carries the highest risk of chronicity
organisms.virulenceFactor: HBx protein promotes carcinogenesis; integration into host DNA; immune-mediated hepatocyte injury rather than direct cytotoxicity
organisms.tooltip: Liver injury is immune-mediated by cytotoxic T cells, not direct viral killing — which is why immunosuppressed patients have less inflammation but more virus. Anti-HBc IgM is the marker in the window period.

organisms.name: Human Papillomavirus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked circular double-stranded DNA; koilocytes with perinuclear halos on cytology; high-risk HPV DNA testing on cervical samples
organisms.manifestations: Common and plantar warts (types 1 and 2), anogenital condyloma acuminatum (6 and 11), cervical, anal, vulvar, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (16 and 18)
organisms.treatment: Cryotherapy, imiquimod, or podophyllin for warts; excisional procedures for cervical dysplasia; nonavalent vaccine for prevention
organisms.transmission: Skin-to-skin and sexual contact; vertical transmission can cause recurrent respiratory papillomatosis
organisms.virulenceFactor: E6 degrades p53 and E7 inactivates Rb, releasing the cell cycle checkpoints and driving malignant transformation
organisms.tooltip: E6 hits p53 and E7 hits Rb — the two-hit knockout of tumor suppressors that explains carcinogenesis. Types 6 and 11 cause warts; 16 and 18 cause cancer.

organisms.name: Parvovirus B19
organisms.labFeatures: The only single-stranded DNA virus, naked icosahedral capsid, smallest DNA virus; infects erythroid progenitors via the P antigen; giant pronormoblasts on marrow
organisms.manifestations: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) with slapped-cheek rash in children; transient aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease; pure red cell aplasia in immunocompromised; hydrops fetalis; arthralgias in adults
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; transfusion for aplastic crisis; IVIG for chronic infection in the immunocompromised; intrauterine transfusion for hydrops
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets and transplacentally; children are contagious before the rash appears and no longer infectious once it does
organisms.virulenceFactor: Tropism for erythroid precursors through the P blood group antigen, halting erythropoiesis for about a week
organisms.tooltip: A week-long halt of erythropoiesis is harmless with a normal 120-day red cell lifespan, but catastrophic in sickle cell disease where survival is already days. Hydrops fetalis if acquired in pregnancy.

organisms.name: Adenovirus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked double-stranded linear DNA with fiber projections from an icosahedral capsid; PCR or antigen detection
organisms.manifestations: Pharyngoconjunctival fever, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (pink eye), febrile pharyngitis, acute hemorrhagic cystitis, gastroenteritis, and pneumonia in military recruits
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; cidofovir for severe disease in the immunocompromised; live oral vaccine used in US military recruits
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets, fecal-oral, and inadequately chlorinated swimming pools; fomites on shared towels and tonometers
organisms.virulenceFactor: Penton base and fiber proteins mediate attachment and cause direct cytotoxicity; E1A and E1B inhibit Rb and p53 in transformation studies
organisms.tooltip: Pool conjunctivitis and military recruit pneumonia are the classic associations. Also a leading cause of hemorrhagic cystitis in children and bone marrow transplant patients.

organisms.name: Molluscum Contagiosum Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Largest DNA virus, enveloped with a complex brick shape, replicates in the cytoplasm (unique for a DNA virus); Henderson-Patterson intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies
organisms.manifestations: Flesh-colored dome-shaped papules with central umbilication; extensive facial lesions in advanced HIV
organisms.treatment: Often self-limited; cryotherapy, curettage, or cantharidin; antiretroviral therapy when HIV-associated
organisms.transmission: Direct skin contact, including sexual contact in adults, and shared towels or gymnasium equipment
organisms.virulenceFactor: Encodes its own DNA-dependent RNA polymerase allowing cytoplasmic replication; viral MC159 blocks apoptosis and immune clearance
organisms.tooltip: Poxviruses are the exception to the rule that DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus — they carry their own RNA polymerase and stay in the cytoplasm. Umbilicated papules are pathognomonic.

organisms.name: Influenza Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (8 segments), helical capsid; rapid antigen or PCR testing; hemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface proteins
organisms.manifestations: Abrupt fever, myalgias, headache, and dry cough; primary viral pneumonia; secondary bacterial pneumonia from S. aureus or pneumococcus; Reye syndrome if given aspirin
organisms.treatment: Oseltamivir or baloxavir within 48 hours; annual inactivated or live attenuated vaccine for prevention
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets and aerosols, with seasonal winter epidemics
organisms.virulenceFactor: Antigenic drift from point mutations causes seasonal epidemics; antigenic shift from reassortment of segmented genomes between species causes pandemics
organisms.tooltip: Drift is minor point mutation causing epidemics; shift is wholesale genome segment reassortment causing pandemics — only segmented viruses can shift. Never give aspirin to febrile children.

organisms.name: Respiratory Syncytial Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped nonsegmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA, helical capsid; multinucleated syncytia in culture; rapid antigen or PCR on nasal wash
organisms.manifestations: Bronchiolitis with wheezing and hyperinflation in infants under two, pneumonia, apnea in young infants, and common cold in adults
organisms.treatment: Supportive care with oxygen and hydration; nirsevimab or palivizumab prophylaxis for high-risk infants; ribavirin rarely in severe immunocompromised cases
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets and fomites, with winter epidemics in daycares and nurseries
organisms.virulenceFactor: F (fusion) protein causes host cell membranes to fuse into multinucleated syncytia and is the target of monoclonal prophylaxis
organisms.tooltip: The leading cause of infant bronchiolitis and hospitalization. The F protein drives syncytia formation and is the target of nirsevimab, which has replaced monthly palivizumab for most infants.

organisms.name: Measles Virus (Rubeola)
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped negative-sense ssRNA, helical capsid; Warthin-Finkeldey multinucleated giant cells; IgM serology or PCR
organisms.manifestations: Prodromal cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots, then a cephalocaudal maculopapular rash; complications include pneumonia, otitis media, encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years later
organisms.treatment: Supportive care plus vitamin A, which reduces mortality; MMR vaccine for prevention; immune globulin for exposed susceptible contacts
organisms.transmission: Airborne aerosols with extraordinary contagiousness — an R0 of 12 to 18 and particles lingering in air for up to two hours
organisms.virulenceFactor: Binds CD150 (SLAM) on lymphocytes causing transient profound immunosuppression and loss of pre-existing immune memory
organisms.tooltip: The three C's — cough, coryza, conjunctivitis — plus Koplik spots precede the rash. Measles erases existing immune memory, which is why children get other infections for years afterward.

organisms.name: Mumps Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped negative-sense ssRNA, helical capsid; elevated serum amylase; IgM serology or buccal swab PCR
organisms.manifestations: Bilateral parotitis, orchitis with risk of infertility, aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, and sensorineural hearing loss
organisms.treatment: Supportive care with analgesia and scrotal support; MMR vaccine for prevention
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets and saliva; outbreaks occur in close-contact settings such as college dormitories even among vaccinated people
organisms.virulenceFactor: Hemagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion proteins mediating entry and syncytia formation in glandular and neural tissue
organisms.tooltip: Mumps makes your parotid glands and testes swell: parotitis, orchitis, aseptic meningitis, and pancreatitis. Elevated amylase can come from the parotid, not just the pancreas.

organisms.name: Rubella Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped positive-sense single-stranded RNA, icosahedral capsid; IgM serology; blueberry muffin rash in congenital cases
organisms.manifestations: Mild fever with a fine pink rash spreading cephalocaudally, postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy, polyarthralgia in adults; congenital rubella syndrome with cataracts, deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus
organisms.treatment: Supportive care only; MMR vaccine for prevention; vaccination is contraindicated in pregnancy as a live vaccine
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets; transplacental transmission with greatest fetal risk in the first trimester
organisms.virulenceFactor: Ability to cross the placenta and disrupt organogenesis, with severity inversely related to gestational age at infection
organisms.tooltip: Congenital rubella triad: cataracts, deafness, and cardiac defects (PDA). Tender postauricular lymphadenopathy is the clue that separates it from measles in a child with a rash.

organisms.name: Rabies Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped bullet-shaped negative-sense ssRNA, helical capsid; Negri bodies as eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in Purkinje and hippocampal neurons; direct fluorescent antibody on brain tissue
organisms.manifestations: Prodromal paresthesias at the bite site, then agitation, hydrophobia, pharyngeal spasms, hypersalivation, and autonomic instability; paralytic form in some; nearly always fatal once symptomatic
organisms.treatment: Postexposure prophylaxis with wound washing, rabies immune globulin infiltrated around the wound, and vaccine series; no effective treatment after symptom onset
organisms.transmission: Bite or saliva contact from bats (most US cases), raccoons, skunks, and dogs worldwide; bat exposure may be unwitnessed
organisms.virulenceFactor: Binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and travels retrograde along axonal microtubules to the CNS, hidden from immune surveillance during the long incubation
organisms.tooltip: The long incubation — weeks to months — reflects slow retrograde axonal transport and is exactly why postexposure prophylaxis works. Negri bodies are the histologic hallmark.

organisms.name: Poliovirus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked positive-sense single-stranded RNA, icosahedral capsid, acid stable so it survives the stomach; CSF shows lymphocytosis with normal glucose; stool culture or PCR
organisms.manifestations: Most infections are asymptomatic or minor febrile illness; aseptic meningitis; asymmetric flaccid paralysis with intact sensation from anterior horn destruction; post-polio syndrome
organisms.treatment: Supportive care and respiratory support; inactivated Salk vaccine or live oral Sabin vaccine for prevention
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, especially where sanitation is poor; the oral vaccine strain can revert and cause vaccine-derived poliomyelitis
organisms.virulenceFactor: Tropism for anterior horn motor neurons via the CD155 receptor, destroying lower motor neurons while sparing sensory pathways
organisms.tooltip: Asymmetric flaccid paralysis with preserved sensation localizes to anterior horn cells. Salk is inactivated and IgG-inducing; Sabin is live, gives mucosal IgA, but can revert to virulence.

organisms.name: Coxsackievirus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked positive-sense ssRNA, icosahedral, acid stable; PCR of throat, stool, or CSF; aseptic meningitis CSF profile
organisms.manifestations: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease, herpangina, myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy, pleurodynia (Bornholm disease), aseptic meningitis, and acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; no specific antiviral
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral and respiratory droplets, with summer and early fall peaks
organisms.virulenceFactor: Direct cytolysis of infected cells and molecular mimicry implicated in autoimmune myocarditis and possibly type 1 diabetes
organisms.tooltip: Coxsackie A causes hand-foot-and-mouth and herpangina; Coxsackie B causes myocarditis, pericarditis, and pleurodynia — 'B for Body and heart.' The leading viral cause of myocarditis.

organisms.name: Rhinovirus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked positive-sense ssRNA, icosahedral capsid, acid labile so it cannot survive the stomach, grows best at 33 C matching nasal temperature; over 100 serotypes
organisms.manifestations: The common cold with rhinorrhea, sneezing, and sore throat; triggers asthma and COPD exacerbations
organisms.treatment: Supportive care only; no vaccine is feasible given serotype diversity
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets, hand-to-nose self-inoculation, and fomites
organisms.virulenceFactor: Binds ICAM-1 on respiratory epithelium; extreme serotype diversity prevents durable immunity and reinfection is lifelong
organisms.tooltip: Acid labile, unlike other picornaviruses, so it cannot establish gut infection — it stays in the nose where 33 C suits it. Over 100 serotypes is why there is no cold vaccine.

organisms.name: Hepatitis A Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked positive-sense ssRNA, icosahedral capsid; anti-HAV IgM indicates acute infection and IgG indicates immunity or vaccination; marked transaminase elevation
organisms.manifestations: Acute hepatitis with jaundice, anorexia, and right upper quadrant pain; never chronic; rarely fulminant in older adults
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; inactivated vaccine for prevention; vaccine or immune globulin for postexposure prophylaxis
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral through contaminated water, raw shellfish, and travel to endemic regions; daycare and food handler outbreaks
organisms.virulenceFactor: Direct hepatocyte infection with immune-mediated injury; naked capsid makes it resistant to bile, acid, and drying
organisms.tooltip: Never becomes chronic and never causes hepatocellular carcinoma — the key contrast with hepatitis B and C. Shellfish and travel are the exam triggers.

organisms.name: Hepatitis C Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped positive-sense ssRNA, icosahedral capsid; anti-HCV antibody screen with HCV RNA confirmation; lacks proofreading so genotypes are highly variable
organisms.manifestations: Usually asymptomatic acute infection with high rate of chronicity; cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; mixed cryoglobulinemia, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, porphyria cutanea tarda, lichen planus
organisms.treatment: Direct-acting antivirals such as sofosbuvir with velpatasvir, curing over 95 percent in 8 to 12 weeks
organisms.transmission: Parenteral — injection drug use is dominant; less efficient sexual and perinatal transmission than hepatitis B
organisms.virulenceFactor: Error-prone RNA polymerase generating quasispecies that outpace antibody responses, explaining the high chronicity rate and absence of a vaccine
organisms.tooltip: No proofreading means constant antigenic variation, which is why 80 percent become chronic and no vaccine exists. Direct-acting antivirals now cure it, so antibody persists while RNA clears.

organisms.name: Hepatitis D Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Defective circular negative-sense ssRNA virus requiring HBsAg as its envelope; anti-HDV antibody and HDV RNA; only infects HBsAg-positive patients
organisms.manifestations: Coinfection with hepatitis B causing severe acute hepatitis; superinfection of chronic hepatitis B causing rapid progression to cirrhosis and fulminant failure
organisms.treatment: Pegylated interferon alfa, or bulevirtide where available; hepatitis B vaccination prevents it entirely
organisms.transmission: Parenteral and sexual, always alongside or on top of hepatitis B infection
organisms.virulenceFactor: Obligate dependence on HBsAg for virion assembly; delta antigen accelerates hepatocyte injury in established hepatitis B
organisms.tooltip: A defective virus that borrows HBsAg as its envelope, so it cannot exist without hepatitis B. Vaccinating against B therefore prevents D. Superinfection is far worse than coinfection.

organisms.name: Hepatitis E Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked positive-sense ssRNA, icosahedral capsid; anti-HEV IgM serology or HEV RNA; waterborne epidemic pattern
organisms.manifestations: Acute hepatitis that is usually self-limited, but with high mortality (up to 20 percent) in pregnant women; chronic infection in solid organ transplant recipients
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; ribavirin for chronic infection in the immunocompromised; no vaccine licensed in most countries
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral via contaminated water in epidemics, and undercooked pork or deer meat in sporadic cases
organisms.virulenceFactor: Direct hepatocyte injury with disproportionate severity in pregnancy, possibly related to hormonal and immune changes
organisms.tooltip: Like hepatitis A it is fecal-oral and does not cause chronic disease in healthy hosts — but unlike A it carries very high mortality in pregnancy, which is the tested distinction.

organisms.name: Rotavirus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked double-stranded segmented RNA (11 segments) with a double-shelled wheel-like capsid; stool antigen immunoassay
organisms.manifestations: Severe watery diarrhea with vomiting and fever in infants and young children, leading to dehydration and metabolic acidosis
organisms.treatment: Oral rehydration solution; live oral vaccine for prevention, given before 15 weeks of age
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, highly contagious in daycare settings, with winter seasonality
organisms.virulenceFactor: NSP4 acts as a viral enterotoxin impairing sodium-glucose cotransport and villous enzyme function, causing osmotic and secretory diarrhea
organisms.tooltip: The only important double-stranded RNA virus. The vaccine must be given early because of an intussusception risk signal that rises with age at first dose.

organisms.name: Norovirus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked positive-sense ssRNA, icosahedral capsid; stool PCR; extremely low infectious dose and environmental resistance
organisms.manifestations: Acute gastroenteritis with prominent vomiting and watery nonbloody diarrhea lasting 24 to 60 hours in all ages
organisms.treatment: Oral or intravenous rehydration; no antiviral or vaccine
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral and vomitus aerosols; cruise ships, schools, and restaurants; resistant to alcohol sanitizers and standard chlorination
organisms.virulenceFactor: Very low infectious dose, environmental stability, rapid antigenic evolution, and binding to histo-blood group antigens determining host susceptibility
organisms.tooltip: The leading cause of adult viral gastroenteritis and of foodborne outbreaks. Alcohol gel does not inactivate it, so soap and water and bleach are needed to stop outbreaks.

organisms.name: Dengue Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped positive-sense ssRNA, icosahedral capsid; NS1 antigen or PCR early, IgM later; thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and hemoconcentration
organisms.manifestations: Breakbone fever with high fever, retro-orbital headache, severe myalgias, and a maculopapular rash; severe dengue with plasma leakage, hemorrhage, and shock
organisms.treatment: Supportive care with careful fluid management; avoid NSAIDs and aspirin given bleeding risk; use acetaminophen
organisms.transmission: Bite of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which bite during the day in urban tropical areas
organisms.virulenceFactor: Antibody-dependent enhancement — non-neutralizing antibody from a prior serotype facilitates uptake of a second serotype into macrophages, worsening disease
organisms.tooltip: Antibody-dependent enhancement explains why second infection with a different serotype is more dangerous than the first — and why vaccine development has been so difficult.

organisms.name: West Nile Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped positive-sense ssRNA, icosahedral capsid; CSF IgM is diagnostic for neuroinvasive disease; birds are the amplifying host
organisms.manifestations: Usually asymptomatic or a mild febrile illness with rash; neuroinvasive disease with encephalitis, meningitis, and a poliomyelitis-like asymmetric flaccid paralysis
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; no specific antiviral or vaccine for humans
organisms.transmission: Culex mosquito bite with birds as reservoir; also transmitted by blood transfusion and organ transplant, so blood is screened
organisms.virulenceFactor: Neuroinvasion across the blood-brain barrier with tropism for anterior horn cells, producing a polio-like syndrome in a minority of patients
organisms.tooltip: Think West Nile when an older adult has encephalitis plus asymmetric flaccid weakness in late summer. Dead crows and jays in the area are the epidemiologic signal.

organisms.name: Zika Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped positive-sense ssRNA; RT-PCR of serum or urine early, serology later with dengue cross-reactivity; fetal ultrasound for microcephaly
organisms.manifestations: Mild fever, maculopapular rash, arthralgia, and nonpurulent conjunctivitis; congenital Zika syndrome with microcephaly and intracranial calcifications; Guillain-Barre syndrome
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; prevention through mosquito avoidance and deferring pregnancy or travel; no vaccine
organisms.transmission: Aedes mosquito bite, sexual contact (notably persisting in semen), and transplacental transmission
organisms.virulenceFactor: Tropism for fetal neural progenitor cells, causing apoptosis and impaired cortical development
organisms.tooltip: The only arbovirus that is also sexually transmitted and persists in semen for months. Congenital infection causes microcephaly with intracranial calcifications.

organisms.name: Yellow Fever Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped positive-sense ssRNA; PCR or serology; Councilman bodies as eosinophilic apoptotic hepatocytes; midzonal hepatic necrosis
organisms.manifestations: Fever with jaundice, black vomit from hemorrhage, bradycardia relative to fever (Faget sign), hepatic and renal failure
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; live attenuated 17D vaccine gives durable protection and is required for entry to some countries
organisms.transmission: Aedes aegypti mosquito bite in urban cycles and forest mosquitoes with monkey reservoirs in jungle cycles
organisms.virulenceFactor: Direct hepatocyte tropism causing midzonal necrosis, with cytokine storm driving shock and coagulopathy
organisms.tooltip: Councilman bodies and midzonal necrosis are the histologic signatures. Faget sign — fever with relative bradycardia — also appears in typhoid and Legionella.

organisms.name: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped diploid positive-sense ssRNA with reverse transcriptase; fourth-generation antigen-antibody immunoassay with RNA confirmation; CD4 count and viral load for staging
organisms.manifestations: Acute retroviral syndrome resembling mononucleosis; years of clinical latency; AIDS with opportunistic infections, wasting, dementia, and malignancies as CD4 falls
organisms.treatment: Combination antiretroviral therapy, typically an integrase inhibitor with two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; tenofovir-emtricitabine for pre-exposure prophylaxis
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact, parenteral exposure including injection drug use, and vertical transmission during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding
organisms.virulenceFactor: gp120 binds CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptors; reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading driving rapid escape mutation; integration into host genome creates a latent reservoir
organisms.tooltip: The latent proviral reservoir in resting memory CD4 cells is why therapy is lifelong and cure remains elusive. CCR5 delta-32 homozygosity confers near-complete resistance to infection.

organisms.name: HTLV-1
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped positive-sense ssRNA retrovirus; serology with Western blot; flower cells (lobulated lymphocytes) on peripheral smear in leukemia
organisms.manifestations: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma with lytic bone lesions and hypercalcemia; HTLV-associated myelopathy (tropical spastic paraparesis) with spastic gait and bladder dysfunction
organisms.treatment: Chemotherapy with zidovudine and interferon for leukemia; supportive and immunomodulatory care for myelopathy; no cure
organisms.transmission: Breastfeeding (the dominant route), sexual contact, and parenteral exposure; endemic in Japan, the Caribbean, and parts of Africa
organisms.virulenceFactor: Tax protein transactivates host genes including IL-2 and its receptor, driving clonal CD4 T-cell proliferation and transformation
organisms.tooltip: Tax is the oncoprotein. Hypercalcemia with lytic lesions plus flower cells on smear in a patient from an endemic region should trigger HTLV-1 testing.

organisms.name: SARS-CoV-2
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped positive-sense ssRNA with helical capsid and crown-like spike projections; RT-PCR or antigen testing; lymphopenia and elevated D-dimer, ferritin, and CRP
organisms.manifestations: Fever, cough, and anosmia; viral pneumonia and ARDS; thromboembolism; multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children; long COVID
organisms.treatment: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir or remdesivir for high-risk outpatients; dexamethasone plus tocilizumab or baricitinib for hypoxemic inpatients; mRNA vaccines for prevention
organisms.transmission: Respiratory aerosols and droplets with substantial presymptomatic transmission
organisms.virulenceFactor: Spike protein binds ACE2 with furin cleavage enhancing entry; blunts interferon response; endothelial infection drives thrombosis
organisms.tooltip: ACE2 is the receptor, which is expressed in nasal epithelium, alveoli, gut, and endothelium — explaining the multisystem involvement and the prominent thrombotic complications.

organisms.name: Ebola Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped filamentous negative-sense ssRNA, helical capsid; RT-PCR of blood; marked transaminase elevation, thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy
organisms.manifestations: Abrupt fever, severe vomiting and diarrhea with massive volume loss, hemorrhage, and multiorgan failure with high case fatality
organisms.treatment: Aggressive fluid and electrolyte resuscitation; monoclonal antibodies inmazeb or ebanga; rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine for outbreak ring vaccination
organisms.transmission: Direct contact with blood or body fluids of symptomatic patients and corpses; bats are the suspected reservoir; not airborne
organisms.virulenceFactor: Glycoprotein-mediated endothelial damage and secreted glycoprotein decoys that absorb antibody; suppression of interferon signaling
organisms.tooltip: Death is usually from hypovolemic shock and electrolyte loss rather than hemorrhage, so aggressive fluid resuscitation markedly improves survival. Patients are not infectious before symptoms.

organisms.name: JC Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked circular double-stranded DNA; CSF PCR for JC virus DNA; MRI shows asymmetric non-enhancing white matter lesions; demyelination with bizarre astrocytes on histology
organisms.manifestations: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy with subacute hemiparesis, visual field deficits, cognitive decline, and ataxia
organisms.treatment: Restore immune function — antiretroviral therapy in HIV, or stopping natalizumab or rituximab; no specific antiviral exists
organisms.transmission: Respiratory or oral acquisition in childhood with lifelong asymptomatic latency in kidney and lymphoid tissue; reactivation with immunosuppression
organisms.virulenceFactor: Latency in kidney and bone marrow with reactivation when cell-mediated immunity fails; tropism for oligodendrocytes causing demyelination
organisms.tooltip: The reason natalizumab requires JC virus antibody screening. Infects oligodendrocytes, so lesions are demyelinating, asymmetric, and characteristically do not enhance with contrast.

organisms.name: BK Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Naked circular dsDNA; plasma and urine BK viral load; decoy cells with ground-glass nuclei in urine; biopsy needed to distinguish nephropathy from rejection
organisms.manifestations: Polyomavirus-associated nephropathy with rising creatinine in kidney transplant recipients; hemorrhagic cystitis and ureteral stenosis after hematopoietic stem cell transplant
organisms.treatment: Reduce immunosuppression, which is the primary intervention; cidofovir or leflunomide have been tried with limited evidence
organisms.transmission: Acquired in childhood through respiratory or oral routes with lifelong latency in renal tubular and urothelial cells
organisms.virulenceFactor: Latency in the urinary tract with reactivation under immunosuppression, producing lytic infection of tubular epithelium
organisms.tooltip: In a kidney transplant patient with rising creatinine, BK nephropathy and acute rejection look alike but need opposite treatment — more immunosuppression versus less — so biopsy is essential.

organisms.name: Parainfluenza Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped nonsegmented negative-sense ssRNA, helical capsid with hemagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion proteins; PCR of nasal specimen
organisms.manifestations: Croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis) with a seal-like barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and steeple sign on neck radiograph; bronchiolitis and pneumonia
organisms.treatment: Supportive care with humidified air; dexamethasone for croup, and nebulized racemic epinephrine for stridor at rest
organisms.transmission: Respiratory droplets and fomites, with fall peaks in young children
organisms.virulenceFactor: Subglottic inflammation and edema in the narrowest part of the pediatric airway, producing stridor disproportionate to the degree of infection
organisms.tooltip: Barking cough with inspiratory stridor and the steeple sign. Epiglottitis differs: thumbprint sign, drooling, and a toxic-appearing child who will not lie down.

organisms.name: Lymphocytic Choriomeningitis Virus
organisms.labFeatures: Enveloped segmented negative-sense ssRNA (two segments) with sandy appearance on electron microscopy; CSF with marked lymphocytosis and low glucose; serology
organisms.manifestations: Aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis after a flu-like prodrome; congenital infection with hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, and periventricular calcifications
organisms.treatment: Supportive care; ribavirin has in vitro activity but is not standard
organisms.transmission: Inhalation or contact with urine, droppings, or saliva of house mice and pet hamsters; transplacental transmission
organisms.virulenceFactor: Persistent infection of rodent reservoirs with heavy viral shedding; immune-mediated meningeal inflammation rather than direct cytolysis
organisms.tooltip: A frequently missed cause of congenital infection that mimics toxoplasmosis with chorioretinitis and intracranial calcifications. Ask about pet rodents or mouse infestation.
